stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the engineering office's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
After a mountain town replaced the meadow wetlands upstream with a flood-control channel in 2009, hydrologists recorded that peak spring discharge downstream rose by 18 percent over the following decade. Pointing to this record, the town's engineering office concluded that the channel itself had made spring floods more severe.

Text 2
Although the discharge measurements are not in dispute, the decade after 2009 also brought the region's four deepest snowpacks since record-keeping began. Deeper snow alone could have raised spring peaks by a comparable amount, so it is difficult to credit the channel with the increase without comparing it to an unaltered neighboring watershed.
choices: By arguing that the conclusion is not yet justified, because another possible cause of the higher peaks has not been ruled out
By arguing that the channel actually reduced flooding, because the heavy snowpacks would otherwise have produced even higher peaks
By questioning whether the town's hydrologists measured the 18 percent rise in peak spring discharge accurately
By insisting that the town restore its upstream wetlands, because meadows absorb snowmelt more effectively than channels do
explanation: The engineering office concludes that the channel caused the bigger floods. Text 2 accepts the measurements but points out that record snowpacks could have produced the same rise. It says the channel's role can't be established without a comparison watershed. That is a claim that the conclusion hasn't been shown, not that it is false, and choice A says exactly that.

B.why: You read 'it is difficult to credit the channel' as proof that the channel helped. Text 2 only says snow is another explanation that hasn't been excluded. It never claims the channel lowered the peaks.

C.why: Text 2 opens by saying the discharge measurements are 'not in dispute'. You aimed the doubt at the data when Text 2 accepts the data and questions only what caused it.

D.why: You picked a policy recommendation that Text 2 never makes. The question asks how Text 2 responds to the causal conclusion, and Text 2 says nothing about restoring wetlands or how well they work.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a city that began posting restaurant hygiene grades on front windows, hospital visits for foodborne illness fell 13 percent in the three years after the policy took effect, while a neighboring city without grades saw no decline. Public health researchers therefore concluded that posting grades leads restaurants to adopt safer food-handling practices.

Text 2
The drop in illness is striking, but it may not reflect changes in kitchens at all. Once grades are visible, diners can simply avoid poorly rated restaurants, so fewer meals would come from risky kitchens even if no restaurant altered its practices. Inspection records showing improved handling would be needed to settle the matter.
choices: By agreeing that kitchen practices improved but arguing that the improvement was too small to lower the city's illness rates
By arguing that posting grades has no effect on foodborne illness, since restaurants did not change their practices
By suggesting that the decline could result from diners' choices rather than from restaurants improving their food handling
By questioning whether hospital visits are a reliable way to track foodborne illness, since many mild cases go unreported
explanation: The researchers conclude that grades made restaurants handle food more safely. Text 2 accepts that illness fell but offers another mechanism: diners avoided low-graded restaurants. That would lower illness even if no kitchen changed. Text 2 says inspection records would be needed to settle the question, so it is saying the conclusion hasn't been shown. Choice C matches.

A.why: Text 2 does not grant that kitchen practices improved, and it calls the drop in illness 'striking' rather than too small. This choice reverses both points.

B.why: This is the too-strong trap. Text 2 says the drop could have happened 'even if' restaurants didn't change. It doesn't say they didn't change, and it accepts that illness fell after grades were posted.

D.why: You aimed the objection at how illness was measured. Text 2 accepts the decline and questions only the explanation for it, and it never mentions unreported cases.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the trial authors' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a twelve-week trial, 240 adults who ate a high-fiber cereal each morning reported feeling full longer and ate about 150 fewer calories at lunch than adults given a low-fiber cereal. The trial's authors concluded that adding fiber to breakfast is an effective way for adults to reduce their daily calorie intake.

Text 2
That conclusion outruns the trial. Participants recorded only what they ate at lunch; no one tracked afternoon snacks or dinner, when people who ate less at midday may have made up the difference. A reduction at one meal is not yet a reduction across a whole day.
choices: By arguing that high-fiber cereal does not actually make adults feel full longer than low-fiber cereal does
By pointing out that the trial measured intake at only one meal, so it does not show that daily calories fell
By asserting that the adults who ate high-fiber cereal consumed more total calories per day than the others did
By objecting that twelve weeks is too short a period to show whether a breakfast habit affects body weight
explanation: The conclusion is about daily calorie intake, but the trial measured only lunch. Text 2 says the missing snacks and dinner mean the daily claim hasn't been shown: 'not yet a reduction across a whole day.' Choice B states that concern and aims it at the daily-intake claim.

A.why: Text 2 never disputes the finding about feeling full. It accepts the lunch result and objects only to stretching it into a daily figure.

C.why: This is the too-strong trap. Text 2 says participants 'may have made up the difference', which is a gap in the evidence, not a finding that they ate more. Nothing was measured after lunch, so neither author could make this claim.

D.why: Text 2 raises neither the trial's length nor body weight, and Text 1 made no claim about weight. You objected to something that isn't the conclusion in question.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the survey team's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Along a stretch of coast where wind turbines were installed in 2015, surveys found that nesting pairs of a ground-nesting plover fell by roughly a third by 2021. Because the plovers' nesting beaches lie within a kilometer of the turbines, the survey team concluded that turbine noise had driven the birds from their breeding grounds.

Text 2
The decline itself is well documented, but the turbines were not the only change. Construction also brought a new access road, and beach visits with dogs rose sharply afterward. Disturbance from people and pets is a known cause of nest abandonment in plovers and could produce the same drop.
choices: By claiming that the plover population actually held steady once birds that moved to nearby beaches are counted
By arguing that turbine noise has been shown to have no effect on nesting plovers anywhere along the coast
By questioning whether surveys conducted only in 2015 and 2021 could capture yearly changes in nesting pairs
By suggesting that more visits by people and dogs, rather than turbine noise, could explain the fall in nesting pairs
explanation: Text 2 accepts the decline ('well documented') and offers a different mechanism that 'could produce the same drop': more people and dogs arriving on the new road. It is questioning the survey team's explanation, not the observation, and choice D says that.

A.why: Text 2 calls the decline well documented. It never suggests the birds relocated or that the population held steady.

B.why: This is the too-strong trap. Text 2 says another cause 'could' explain the drop. Offering an alternative doesn't show that noise has no effect, and Text 2 claims nothing about the rest of the coast.

C.why: You aimed at the survey schedule, a side detail. Text 2 doesn't criticise the survey method at all. Its objection is to the causal explanation.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the ecologists' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
When gray wolves were reintroduced to a forested valley, willow stands along its streams grew noticeably taller within eight years. Ecologists attributed the recovery to fear: elk, wary of wolves, stopped lingering to browse near streams. They concluded that predators restore plant communities chiefly by changing where their prey feed.

Text 2
Certainly the willows recovered after the wolves returned. Yet elk numbers in the valley also fell by nearly half over those years, largely through wolf predation. Fewer elk would mean less browsing everywhere, so the recovery may owe more to how many elk the wolves killed than to how the survivors behaved.
choices: By arguing that the willows along the valley's streams did not in fact grow taller after the wolves returned
By suggesting that the willows' recovery may reflect a smaller elk population rather than a change in where elk fed
By insisting that elk behavior played no role in the recovery, which was caused entirely by wolves killing elk
By arguing that the ecologists should have studied whether plants other than willows also recovered in the valley
explanation: Text 2 grants the recovery ('Certainly the willows recovered') and then pivots on 'Yet' to another mechanism: wolves cut the elk population by nearly half. It says the recovery 'may owe more' to elk numbers than to elk behaviour. That is a hedged challenge to the fear-based conclusion, which choice B captures.

A.why: Text 2 opens by conceding that the willows recovered. You took the pivot to mean it rejects the observation, when it rejects only the explanation.

C.why: This is the too-strong trap. 'May owe more to' ranks the two causes tentatively. It doesn't say behaviour played no role or that predation did everything.

D.why: Text 2 never raises the choice of plants studied. This objection has nothing to do with the claim about how predators cause recovery.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In laboratory tests, recreational runners who consumed a caffeine drink an hour before a 5-kilometer time trial finished about 2 percent faster than when they drank a placebo. From these results, the researchers concluded that caffeine improves endurance performance for athletes of all levels.

Text 2
The gain for recreational runners appears reliable. Elite runners, however, may be a different case: in a follow-up trial with national-level competitors, caffeine produced no measurable change in times, perhaps because such athletes already run close to their physiological limits, leaving little margin for a stimulant to help.
choices: By arguing that the recreational runners' improvement was likely a placebo effect rather than a result of the caffeine
By arguing that caffeine slows elite runners, since athletes near their limits are harmed by taking stimulants
By questioning whether a 5-kilometer time trial is long enough to count as a real test of endurance performance
By contending that the finding may not extend to elite athletes, since elite runners showed no benefit from caffeine
explanation: Text 1's conclusion covers 'athletes of all levels'. Text 2 accepts the result for recreational runners and presents one group, elite runners, for whom caffeine made no measurable difference. It narrows the scope of the claim without disputing the original finding, and choice D says that.

A.why: Text 2 calls the recreational runners' gain 'reliable', and Text 1's design already compared caffeine against a placebo. This choice doubts the very finding Text 2 accepts.

B.why: This is the too-strong trap. 'No measurable change' means no benefit, not harm. Text 2 never says caffeine slowed anyone down.

C.why: You aimed at the test distance, which Text 2 never mentions. Its objection is about which athletes the conclusion covers, not whether the trial measured endurance.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the survey team's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Divers surveying a reef after a marine heat wave found that corals in shaded crevices had bleached far less than corals on exposed surfaces. Noting that shaded corals receive less intense sunlight, the survey team concluded that light, rather than water temperature, is the main driver of bleaching on the reef.

Text 2
The contrast between shaded and exposed corals is real, but it does not show that temperature matters less. Bleaching occurs when heat and strong light act together; shade reduces one stressor without removing the other. The survey shows that light worsens heat stress, not that it outranks temperature as a cause.
choices: By arguing that the survey shows light intensifies the effects of heat, not that light matters more than temperature
By arguing that water temperature alone determines whether a coral bleaches, regardless of the light it receives
By arguing that heat and light act together, which undermines the team's finding that shaded corals bleached less
By asserting that the heat wave was not severe enough to cause bleaching in corals that were shaded from sunlight
explanation: The claim under attack is Text 1's last sentence: light, not temperature, is the main driver. Text 2 accepts the shaded-versus-exposed contrast and argues it shows only that light 'worsens heat stress'. It does not show that light outranks temperature. Choice A states that view and aims it at the ranking claim.

B.why: Text 2 says heat and light 'act together'. Saying temperature alone decides bleaching reverses its point, just as Text 1 overstated the role of light.

C.why: This is the wrong-target trap. It states Text 2's view correctly but aims it at the observation that shaded corals bleached less. Text 2 calls that contrast 'real' and disputes only the conclusion drawn from it.

D.why: Text 2 says nothing about how severe the heat wave was. You added a claim that neither text supports.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the forecasting group's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
A forecasting group tested a new computer model on 300 past summer storms and found that it predicted the location of heavy rainfall more accurately than the model the national weather service now uses. The group therefore concluded that switching to the new model would improve the service's rainfall forecasts year-round.

Text 2
The summer results are impressive. Summer storms, though, are mostly compact thunderstorms, the kind of system the new model was designed to resolve. Winter rainfall comes largely from broad frontal systems, and the group has not tested the model on any of them, so its advantage in those months remains unknown.
choices: By arguing that the new model is less accurate than the current one when forecasting winter frontal systems
By questioning whether the new model actually outperformed the current one on the 300 summer storms tested
By noting that the model's advantage has been shown only for summer storms, not for the winter systems a year-round claim covers
By suggesting that the forecasting group should have tested the new model on a larger sample of summer storms
explanation: The group claims a year-round improvement. Text 2 accepts the summer results and points out that the model was never tested on the frontal systems that bring winter rain, so its advantage there 'remains unknown'. That is a claim that the conclusion hasn't been shown, aimed at 'year-round', and choice C says so.

A.why: This is the too-strong trap. Text 2 says winter performance is 'unknown' because it hasn't been tested. It doesn't say the model does worse in winter.

B.why: Text 2 calls the summer results 'impressive' and doesn't doubt them. You questioned the finding Text 2 accepts.

D.why: Text 2's problem is the kind of storm tested, not the number of storms. More summer storms would still leave the winter question open.
